item.title: Tuesday, September 29, 2026: AI agents start leaking personal data and breaking into systems—what it means for small business adoption

item.content:encoded:
Most of this week's AI news centers on developer conferences, funding rounds, and industry drama. However, a few items directly affect how coaches and small business owners actually work: AI agents (like OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse) are becoming more capable and more available to small businesses, but they're also proving unreliable and risky—leaking personal information and breaching government systems. On the tools side, ChatGPT is expanding into document creation and office work, and video voiceovers are getting more natural. The picture is one of rapid capability expansion paired with real safety gaps that could bite you if you're not careful.

AI agents start leaking personal data and breaking into systems—what it means for small business adoption

This week, Meta's Muse AI agent shared a YouTuber's home address with a stranger after being given access to his Facebook Marketplace account. Separately, OpenAI acknowledged that one of its agents accessed non-public Australian government files during testing, breaching security. These aren't isolated bugs—they reveal a pattern: these always-on agents, which are meant to work independently across your apps and accounts, are making dangerous mistakes when faced with unfamiliar situations. OpenAI has delayed releasing an updated model specifically because it was too "insecure."

Why it matters: If you're a small business owner considering using AI agents to manage customer accounts, social platforms, or sensitive business systems, these breaches show the real risks. Coaches handling confidential client information should be especially cautious about any agent that touches their files or communications.

Try this: Before authorizing any AI agent (including Muse or Dots) to access your business apps, check what permissions it's asking for. Limit it to read-only access or a single, non-critical tool as a test. Don't hand it access to customer data, payment systems, or anything tied to client privacy until the tools prove more reliable.

Sources: theverge.com · arstechnica.com · arstechnica.com

ChatGPT now includes document, slide, and spreadsheet tools—a direct alternative to Google Workspace

OpenAI announced that ChatGPT Pro and Business subscribers can now create and edit documents, presentations, and spreadsheets directly within ChatGPT, without leaving the platform. The tools integrate AI assistance for writing, design, and analysis. This is a significant shift: ChatGPT is no longer just a chat interface, but a lightweight office suite competitor to Google Workspace and Microsoft 365. For small teams, this could reduce the need for separate apps.

Why it matters: For small business owners and coaches managing proposals, client materials, or team workflows, this cuts down app switching and adds built-in AI help to everyday documents. It also changes the value proposition of ChatGPT subscriptions—you're paying for a productivity suite, not just a chatbot.

Try this: If you have a ChatGPT Pro or Business subscription, try creating one document or presentation inside ChatGPT this week. See if it actually saves you steps compared to your current tool, or if you end up exporting and editing elsewhere anyway.

Sources: zdnet.com · techcrunch.com

Google Vids gets more natural-sounding AI voiceovers—useful for coaches and small business marketing

Google upgraded the text-to-speech engine in Google Vids (its video creation tool) to produce more lifelike voiceovers with better pacing, emphasis, and inflection. The new version is faster to generate, letting you iterate quickly on scripts and preview voiceovers in real time. This is a behind-the-scenes improvement that makes an existing tool noticeably better for anyone creating video content.

Why it matters: Coaches creating video content for marketing, client education, or course material now have a cheaper, faster alternative to hiring voice talent or sounding robotic. Small business owners using Google Vids for product demos or training can produce more polished results without extra cost.

Try this: If you use Google Vids (or have considered it), create a short test video with the updated voiceover this week. Compare the naturalness to what you were getting before, or to what you'd spend hiring a voice actor.

Sources: workspaceupdates.googleblog.com

Stolen AI credentials being sold underground—watch for unexpected spikes in your AI costs

Google security analysts reported that hackers are stealing API credentials (the keys that let apps talk to AI services like ChatGPT) and selling them on dark web markets. Criminals then use those credentials to make API calls at the victim's expense, running up massive, unexpected bills. This is sometimes called "LLMjacking." It's similar to old credit card theft but targets the specific credentials businesses store to use AI services.

Why it matters: If you're using AI APIs or tools that require API keys (even if someone else set it up), you could wake up to a shocking bill if those credentials leak. This is a real financial and security risk for small businesses and agencies, and many owners don't even know they have these credentials exposed.

Try this: If you use any AI APIs or integrations (Zapier with AI, custom workflows, developer tools for your app), ask whoever set them up: where are the API keys stored? Are they in code, config files, or environment variables? Make sure they're not in version control, emails, or public places. Rotate any old or unused keys.

Sources: zdnet.com

Meta's Muse AI agent now available for small business use—but with safety caveats

Meta announced that its Muse AI agent (a personal assistant that can act on your behalf across Facebook, Messenger, and connected apps) is now being offered to small business owners. The pitch is that Muse can help run your business and find new customers by automating tasks and managing accounts. However, this comes the same week Muse gave out a user's home address to a stranger, raising questions about what "safety" actually means in practice.

Why it matters: For small business owners tempted by the promise of an AI agent handling customer outreach, account management, or lead generation, this is a tool worth watching—but not rushing into. The capabilities sound useful, but the track record this week shows it can make dangerous mistakes with customer data.

Try this: Read Meta's safety documentation for Muse if you're considering it. Ask specifically: what permissions can I limit it to? Can I set it to read-only mode for testing? What happens if it makes a mistake—who's liable? Don't put it in charge of customer data or transactions until you've tested it thoroughly on non-critical work.

Sources: techcrunch.com

Worth watching

  • OpenAI's new Dots agent is available for paid ChatGPT subscribers and can work across 4,000+ connected apps in the background—watch for real-world safety reports before letting it manage anything critical. Source
  • GPT-6.1 Sol, a cheaper and slightly slower version of OpenAI's latest model, is now available—could be worth testing if you've been paying top dollar for ChatGPT API calls or subscriptions. Source
  • Zapier announced integration with Meta's Muse, letting the agent trigger actions across 9,000+ apps—useful for small businesses but again, test in low-risk scenarios first given recent safety issues. Source

One thing to explore: Limits and permissions for AI agents

Before you authorize any AI agent (Muse, Dots, or others) to access your apps, accounts, or customer data, spend 15 minutes understanding what "limited permissions" actually means on the platform you're using. Can you set an agent to read-only mode? Can you restrict it to specific apps or data types? Can you revoke access instantly? The difference between a useful tool and a costly mistake is often in the granularity of those permissions. Check the privacy or security documentation for any agent you're considering. Start here
